A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UMAD research. Their main text, appendices, equations, algorithms, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original debate experiments, uncertainty and answer-flipping analyses, and UMAD training results, including Table 1 and Figures 1–6.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses, revises Table 1 results, and adds component ablations and a Single-GRPO Pair comparison in Table 3.

M1.justification: UMAD retains the same GRPO-based training procedure, standardized NLL advantage weighting, and peer-correctness intrinsic reward. Algorithm 2 is unchanged. The revised descriptions of these signals as operational proxies do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Both versions train on MATH and evaluate on MATH500, GSM8K, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25. The homogeneous and heterogeneous Qwen/Llama diagnostic coverage is retained. The new ablations use existing tasks and model pairings.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Zero-Shot MAD and Standard IPPO. New Table 3 adds independently trained Single-GRPO Pair agents and Intrinsic-only and NLL-only variants, substantially extending the comparisons needed to distinguish debate co-training from standalone training and individual uncertainty components.

E3.justification: For AIME, v2 increases response/prompt limits from the previously stated 2,048/5,120 tokens to 4,096/9,216, materially changing evaluation conditions. The new Single-GRPO baseline receives 15 training epochs versus UMAD's retained two. Section 3.2 also changes the stated rollout count from 16 to five, although Appendix D.5 retains 16; the actual diagnostic sampling protocol remains inconsistent.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.1 and Table 3 separately test the intrinsic reward and NLL weighting and examine whether standalone GRPO training explains the gains. Conversely, v1's two dialogue case studies illustrating homogeneous failure and heterogeneous success are removed. The existing uncertainty trajectories, flipping analysis, and longer-debate evaluation remain.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 provides point estimates without evaluation seed counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 adds uncertainty throughout Table 1 and specifies five evaluation seeds, while Table 3 reports three-seed means and standard deviations. Identical UMAD entries appear in both tables despite these differing seed descriptions, leaving their statistical provenance unclear.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises AIME results and heterogeneous UMAD scores. At T=5, UMAD's heterogeneous agent averages change from 50.6/57.7 to 66.5/65.8; the stronger agent now trails IPPO's 67.4 average. Table 3 adds component and GRPO comparison results. These are revised reports under changed AIME budgets and seed reporting, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: v1's Theorem 3.3 claims a marginal information-gain ordering from a conditional novelty assumption, while its proof compares message pairs. v2 replaces it with homogeneous saturation Assumption 3.3 and Theorem 3.4, explicitly bounding the joint-information advantage by Delta, with a matching proof in Appendix B.3. The earlier individual-agent entropy/KL derivation is also removed.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the contribution as an operational, answer-level uncertainty framework. The claim of independent reasoning superiority over single-agent RL is replaced by a claim about post-debate performance and peer-information utilization. This materially narrows what the framework and training results are claimed to establish.

C2.justification: v2 expands the earlier proxy caveats, distinguishing latent beliefs, answer-level diagnostics, and training signals. It explicitly limits the heterogeneity theorem to information potential, acknowledges that the stronger agent is not uniformly improved, and discusses compatible model pairings. Appendix J adds substantive limits concerning mathematical tasks, answer equivalence, and extension beyond exact-match verification.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code location, documents the Single-GRPO training budget and AIME length exceptions, and changes the computational-resources training group size from 16 to five, matching Table 2 in both versions. Existing pseudocode, prompts, hardware information, and most hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of identity-aware debate, ModeX, and Tang et al.'s uncertainty-driven policy optimization, plus a Llama reference. It removes the Kadavath and Tomov references and the earlier first-work assertion. Most other bibliography changes concern the same works' publication metadata; the principal research positioning remains uncertainty analysis coupled with MARL.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, method explanation, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work is condensed in the main text and reorganized into Appendix A; limitations move from Section 8 to Appendix J. Dialogue examples are removed, an ablation appendix is introduced, and author/publication information is updated.

P2.justification: Table 1 is regrouped by debate round and gains comparison coloring and an expanded caption; Table 3 is added and the dialogue-example boxes disappear. All six figures retain the same underlying graphics, with localized caption and placement changes. The overall visual format remains stable.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the central heterogeneity theorem's statement–proof mismatch, better distinguishes operational proxies from Bayesian quantities, and adds previously missing component and standalone-RL controls in Table 3. These changes substantially strengthen the paper's theoretical validity and empirical argument. Conflicting seed and rollout descriptions still limit reproducibility, and dialogue examples are lost, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvements.
